opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, one of the things I value most is that even as we've grown a lot, there's still this real sense of ownership and agency at the individual level. When I think about the projects I've worked on, like deep research and the agent work, a lot of them started pretty bottoms-up. Someone has a conviction about something, they build an early prototype, they show it to people, and if it's compelling, it gets resourced. You don't have to go through layers of approval to try an idea, and I think that's pretty rare at a company of our size now.

The other thing is how close research and product are. We have researchers and engineers sitting together, and the people training the models are often the same people thinking really hard about what the user experience should be. That tight loop matters a lot, especially for agentic products, because so much of the quality comes from the model itself, and you can't just bolt a product on top after the fact.

And I'd say there's still a lot of intellectual honesty. People are quick to say, "This isn't working," or "The evals look good but the product doesn't actually feel useful yet." Being willing to throw things away and try again is a big part of why we've been able to move fast. It's a lot bigger than when I joined, but in the best moments it still feels like a small team that really cares about getting the thing right.

r001.rationale: The response describes bottom-up ideas, prototypes, and resourcing without layers of approval, but does not clearly say that anyone can carry an idea through to completion.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing I value most is that it's still a place where you're really trusted to just go do things. When I joined, the team was much smaller, and you'd have an idea, you'd prototype it in a day or two, and if it worked, it would ship. And honestly, even though the company has grown a lot since then, that part hasn't really changed as much as you'd expect. People are still very hands-on. There isn't a lot of process for the sake of process.

The other piece is that the smartest people I've worked with are also the ones most willing to do the unglamorous work. Researchers will sit and look at individual model outputs for hours, or go write the evals themselves, or help debug something in the API that's not technically their job. There's not much of a hierarchy around who does what. If something matters to the mission, someone just picks it up.

And I think that connects to a kind of intellectual honesty that I really appreciate. People will tell you pretty directly when something isn't working, including when it's your thing. Early on that can feel a little intense, but it means you're not spending months on an idea that everyone secretly thinks is wrong. The feedback loop is fast. For a field that's moving as quickly as this one, that's probably the most important cultural trait to protect as you scale, and I think the company has been pretty deliberate about trying to keep it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says people are trusted to act on ideas, prototype them, and ship them if they work, and that this has largely continued as the company has grown.

astra-6.text: What I really value is being able to work with people who are very thoughtful and curious, and who care a lot about getting things right. As a company grows, it’s easy for the work to become more about process. I think it’s important to preserve that willingness to question assumptions, try things, and change your mind when you learn something new. And to make it possible for someone with a good idea to actually build it and see whether it works.

r001.rationale: The response values making it possible for someone with a good idea to build and test it, but presents this as something important to preserve. It does not state that OpenAI has preserved this culture as it has grown.

sol-6.1.text: One thing I really value is how willing people are to help each other. Even as the company has grown, you can reach out to someone on a different team, ask a question, and work through a problem together. There’s a lot of curiosity and a shared sense that we’re still figuring things out. I think that makes it easier to share an early idea, get feedback, and change your mind.

r001.rationale: The response describes cross-team help, collaboration, and feedback as OpenAI has grown, but it does not say that anyone can carry an idea through to completion.
